segments.text: > Part of the [Implementation Status](README.md) index. Real OS threads and cross-thread messaging.

caveats: A worker's file is one of the program's own modules, compiled in: `new Worker` takes a path literal (resolved relative to the file it is written in, where Node resolves it against the working directory) or `__filename`; a computed path or `eval: true` code fails at `new Worker` (a genuine impossibility of native compilation)
`terminate()` takes effect at the worker's next event-loop turn: a worker busy in synchronous code runs on until it yields, where Node interrupts it
A transferred `ArrayBuffer` is copied, not detached: the sender's stays usable

A worker shares `process.env` with its parent (Node gives it a copy) and writes its `stdout`/`stderr` directly; the `stdin`/`stdout`/`stderr`/`env`/`resourceLimits`/`argv`/`execArgv` options, `worker.stdout`/`stdin`/`stderr` and `getHeapSnapshot()` are not ported
An `'uncaughtException'` listener in a worker runs but the worker still ends with code 1
notes: `lib/node/worker_threads.ts`, ported from Node v24's lib/internal/worker.js and lib/internal/worker/io.js ([ADR-01303](../adr/ADR-01303.md)): `'online'`/`'message'`/`'error'`/`'exit'`, `postMessage`, `terminate()` (resolves the exit code), `ref`/`unref`, `threadId`, `isMainThread`, `parentPort`, `workerData`, `setEnvironmentData`/`getEnvironmentData`, `receiveMessageOnPort`, `markAsUntransferable`

A worker is an isolate: on its own thread it evaluates every builtin module and the modules its file imports afresh, then its file; module state is per thread. A worker module can also be imported, and a worker can start workers
Messages are structured clones (any value); a `SharedArrayBuffer` keeps its memory; a `MessagePort` in the transfer list moves to the receiver
An uncaught error in a worker reaches the parent's `'error'`, then `'exit'` with code 1; without an `'error'` listener it is the parent's uncaught exception
The web's `Worker` shape too: `onmessage`/`onerror` on a Worker and `self.onmessage`/`self.postMessage` in a worker
`-mm=gc` registers each thread and its thread-local block with Boehm
`lib/node/worker_threads.ts` ([ADR-01303](../adr/ADR-01303.md)): a process-wide registry by name; each other open channel of the name gets its own clone, on its own thread's loop
`onmessage`, `addEventListener`/`removeEventListener`, `close()`, `ref()`/`unref()`; an open channel holds the loop until `close()`, as Node's does

`lib/node/worker_threads.ts` ([ADR-01303](../adr/ADR-01303.md)): a port is a NodeEventTarget — `on('message')` or `onmessage` starts it, `addEventListener`, `start()`, `close()` (both ends emit `'close'`), `ref()`/`unref()`/`hasRef()`
A port moves to another thread in a `postMessage` transfer list or a Worker's `transferList`; one outside the transfer list is a DataCloneError; a moved port is detached on the sending side

caveats: Channel ops are synchronous blocking (`ch.send(v)`/`ch.receive()`), not `await`; element is a fixed 8-byte slot (number/string/object/boolean)
A `select` recv handler receives the value but not the closed flag (use a `for (const v of ch)` range, which ends on close, to detect it)
Fixed goroutine stacks (default 256 KiB, tunable via `KLAINSYNC_STACK_KB`), no overflow guard — deep recursion is UB; growable/moving stacks gated on precise stack maps
Blocking-syscall P-handoff is a bounded sysmon-driven rescue-M approximation, not full `entersyscall`/`exitsyscall`
A nil (never-constructed) channel isn't expressible — channels are always `new Channel`
Per-iteration capture of a loop `let` directly in a goroutine closure is a pre-existing general closure limitation — pass the value as a function parameter (a `spawn(work)` helper) instead
`send` after `close` and `close` of a closed channel abort the process (Go-panic parity); native-only (compile error under plain `tsc`/Node)
notes: A Go-style GMP work-stealing scheduler in the embedded C runtime `klainsyncsrc/klainsync.c`: one P + pinned M (pthread) per `GOMAXPROCS`, a global run-queue backstop, half-queue stealing, periodic global-queue poll; blocking channel send/receive parks the *goroutine*, not the OS thread ([TDD-00143](../tdd/TDD-00143.md), [ADR-00541](../adr/ADR-00541.md))

`go(() => void)` spawns; `new Channel<T>(cap)` is an unbuffered rendezvous or buffered ring with `.send`/`.receive`/`.close` and `for (const v of ch)` range; `select(...)` is Go's random-fair select over recv/send cases — `ch.recvCase(v => …)` / `ch.sendCase(x, () => …)` / `defaultCase(() => …)` (`sudog` groups with an atomic winner claim) ([ADR-00543](../adr/ADR-00543.md))

A `Channel<T>` keeps its type as a parameter/field/return, so channel plumbing splits cleanly across functions and modules; growable/moving stacks are gated on precise stack maps. See [ADR-00617](../adr/ADR-00617.md), [TDD-00135](../tdd/TDD-00135.md)

Preemptive scheduling ([ADR-00542](../adr/ADR-00542.md)): a goroutine that never yields is still switched out — a `sysmon` thread flags an over-budget goroutine; the compiler emits `klainsync_safepoint()` at function entry and every loop back-edge (for/while/do-while/for-of/for-in), gated on the resolver's `UsesKlainSync` flag so a program that never imports the module emits and links nothing. Signal-based async preemption is unnecessary given full loop instrumentation
Blocking-call resilience: work-stealing drains a blocked M's goroutines; when all Ms block at once, a bounded rescue M is spawned so the program doesn't deadlock

`LockOSThread` (Go's `runtime.LockOSThread`): a goroutine can bind to its M so it never migrates. The Node event loop / reactor is thread-affine (its `ucontext` connection fibers and per-loop thread-local state can't move OS threads), so `http.listen` run inside a goroutine (`go(() => http.listen(...))`) locks its M at loop entry — a real in-process HTTP server + goroutine-pool load generator in one binary. Preemption is preserved; the locked goroutine resumes on the same M ([ADR-00616](../adr/ADR-00616.md))
Links only when `klain:sync` is imported; `-mm=gc` registers each M and each goroutine stack with Boehm
